rows: Employers have a legal duty to protect employees from work-related stress by assessing the risk and acting on it.
HSE's Management Standards provide a step-by-step framework for assessing and improving work-related stress controls.
The Management Standards cover demands, control, support, relationships, role and organisational change.
Poorly managed workload, work patterns and the work environment can contribute to work-related stress.
Lack of control, inadequate support, conflict, role uncertainty and poorly managed change are recognised stressors.
Employers should share stress-risk assessment findings with workers and manage identified physical and mental health risks.
The Management Standards encourage worker consultation and use of surveys, existing data and discussion to identify improvements.
HSE provides tools, templates, workbooks and case studies for work-related stress prevention.
General stress guidance does not prove that a particular workplace or individual has harmful exposure.
Risk depends on work design, management practice, worker circumstances and current evidence rather than a property address.
Employers must control health risks from welding fume even where welding is only a small part of the job.
HSE states that all welding fume can cause lung cancer and can also cause asthma and other health conditions.
The control hierarchy starts with avoiding or reducing welding-fume exposure.
Local exhaust ventilation should capture welding fume at source for indoor work where welding cannot be avoided.
Suitable respiratory protective equipment is required where extraction alone does not achieve adequate control.
Welding-fume controls must be kept effective, checked for damage and repaired when faulty.
Local exhaust ventilation systems require competent thorough examination and testing at least every 14 months.
Respiratory health surveillance may be required where the risk assessment identifies a reasonable likelihood of occupational asthma.
The presence of welding activity does not by itself demonstrate the worker's actual dose or control performance.
Exposure depends on process, duration, metal, consumable, ventilation, extraction, RPE fit and work practice.
Pressure-system users must provide safe and suitable equipment installed and used for its intended purpose.
Users need to know the relevant fluid, operating conditions and safe operating limits of pressure equipment.
Suitable protective devices such as safety valves or bursting discs must function correctly.
A whole-system maintenance programme should account for equipment age, use and operating environment.
The Pressure Systems Safety Regulations aim to prevent serious injury from stored energy released by system failure.
A suitable written scheme of examination must be in place before qualifying equipment is operated.
A competent person must examine the system in accordance with the written scheme.
Pressure equipment placed on the market must satisfy applicable essential safety and conformity requirements.
General pressure-system guidance does not verify the integrity or examination status of a specific installation.
Applicability depends on system design, fluid, pressure, exclusions and legal dutyholder responsibilities.
The Control of Lead at Work regime requires employers to prevent or adequately control occupational exposure to lead.
Lead exposure can affect blood, the nervous system, kidneys, fertility and blood pressure.
Employers should reduce the number of people exposed, the amount of lead and the duration of exposure.
Engineering, respiratory, administrative and behavioural controls must be used correctly and maintained.
Employers should keep records demonstrating that lead-exposure controls remain effective.
The approved code covers handling, processing, repair, maintenance, storage and disposal activities liable to expose workers.
Lead may present inhalation, ingestion or skin-absorption hazards depending on its physical and chemical form.
Appropriate medical surveillance should be discussed with an HSE-appointed doctor where the regulations require it.
The presence of an older building or lead-containing material does not establish significant occupational exposure.
Actual risk depends on lead form, task, airborne concentration, hygiene, controls and medical-surveillance criteria.
